title: Ἑλένης μαντεία καὶ μάντις Θεοκλύμενος
titleEn: Helen's Omen and the Seer from Argos — Odyssey 15.172–259
part: Helen's Omen and the Seer from Argos (15.172–259)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Helen finishes reading the omen of the eagle and the goose: as the eagle seized the goose, Odysseus will come home and take vengeance on the suitors, or is perhaps there already. Telemachus answers with a wish that it may be so, and he and Peisistratus drive hard for Pylos, spending the night at Pherae in the house of Diocles. At Pylos Telemachus asks Peisistratus to leave him at the ship, lest Nestor keep him against his will. Peisistratus agrees, unloads the gifts at the ship, and urges him aboard, and Telemachus orders his crew to make ready. While he is sacrificing to Athena at the stern, a seer on the run from Argos comes up, and the poet gives the man's descent, through Mantius and Polypheides, from Melampus, before he is named as Theoclymenus and begins to speak to Telemachus.

sentences.t: κλῦτέ μευ·
sentences.tr: klyte meu·
sentences.l: “Hear me;
sentences.i: “Hear me;
sentences.n: κλῦτε is the aorist imperative plural of κλύω 'hear', here with the genitive μευ (= μου, 'me'); the plural shows that Helen is speaking to more than one person. Her interpretation of the eagle and the goose begins here: the previous part ends with the line that introduces her, and the opening quotation mark is printed in this unit.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ μαντεύσομαι, ὡς ἐνὶ θυμῷ
ἀθάνατοι βάλλουσι καὶ ὡς τελέεσθαι ὀΐω.
sentences.tr:
autar egō manteusomai, hōs eni thymōi
athanatoi ballousi kai hōs teleesthai oïō.
sentences.l:
but I will prophesy, as in (my) heart
the immortals are casting (it), and as I think it will be fulfilled.
sentences.i: But I will prophesy as the immortals cast it into my heart, and as I think it will be fulfilled.
sentences.n: μαντεύσομαι is the future of μαντεύομαι 'prophesy, divine', with ἐγώ stressing the speaker. ὡς … ὡς is 'as … and as': she says how the gods put the meaning into her mind and how she thinks it will be fulfilled. βάλλουσι 'they cast' has no expressed object, so 'it' (the thought) is understood; ἐνὶ is ἐν, and the Greek has no 'my' with θυμῷ: it is understood from the speaker. A seer claims that the gods themselves put the meaning of a sign into her mind. τελέεσθαι is the uncontracted passive infinitive of τελέω 'fulfil' (Attic τελεῖσθαι), with future sense after ὀΐω 'I think, I suppose'.

sentences.t:
ὡς ὅδε χῆν’ ἥρπαξ’ ἀτιταλλομένην ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
ἐλθὼν ἐξ ὄρεος, ὅθι οἱ γενεή τε τόκος τε,
ὣς Ὀδυσεὺς κακὰ πολλὰ παθὼν καὶ πόλλ’ ἐπαληθεὶς
οἴκαδε νοστήσει καὶ τίσεται·
sentences.tr:
hōs hode chēn’ hērpax’ atitallomenēn eni oikōi
elthōn ex oreos, hothi hoi geneē te tokos te,
hōs Odyseus kaka polla pathōn kai poll’ epalētheis
oikade nostēsei kai tisetai·
sentences.l:
as this one a goose snatched, being reared in the house,
coming from the mountain, where for him kindred and brood are,
so Odysseus, many evils having suffered and much having wandered,
home will return and take vengeance;
sentences.i: As this eagle came from the mountain, where its kin and its brood are, and snatched a goose that was being reared in the house, so Odysseus, after suffering many evils and wandering far, will return home and take vengeance;
sentences.n: ὡς … ὣς is the comparison 'as … so'. ὅδε is 'this one here': it points to the eagle of the omen, just seen, and the English says 'eagle'. ἥρπαξ’ is the elided aorist of ἁρπάζω 'snatch'; ἀτιταλλομένην is the passive participle of ἀτιτάλλω 'rear, tend', agreeing with χῆν’ (χῆνα, 'goose'). ὄρεος is the genitive of ὄρος with Ionic -εος (Attic ὄρους); ὅθι is 'where'; οἱ is 'for him', the dative of possession, and γενεή 'family, kin' and τόκος 'offspring, brood' are the two things the eagle has waiting at home. παθών is the aorist participle of πάσχω, and ἐπαληθείς the aorist passive participle of ἐπαλάομαι 'wander about'. νοστήσει is the future of νοστέω 'come home', from νόστος; οἴκαδε has the -δε of direction. τίσεται is the future middle of τίνω, 'exact a penalty, take vengeance', with no object: the suitors are not named until line 178.

sentences.t:
ἠὲ καὶ ἤδη
οἴκοι, ἀτὰρ μνηστῆρσι κακὸν πάντεσσι φυτεύει.
sentences.tr:
ēe kai ēdē
oikoi, atar mnēstērsi kakon pantessi phyteuei.
sentences.l:
or even now
at home, and for all the suitors evil he is planting.”
sentences.i: or he is even now at home, and is devising evil for all the suitors.”
sentences.n: ἠέ is 'or' and brings in a second possibility: Odysseus may not merely come later but may be home already. The verb is left out: understand 'he is' with οἴκοι 'at home'. ἀτάρ is 'and, but', joining the second clause. φυτεύει 'plants, sows' is used of devising evil; κακόν is singular, 'evil', and πάντεσσι is the long epic dative plural of πᾶς (Attic πᾶσι), agreeing with μνηστῆρσι 'for the suitors'. The closing quotation mark ends Helen's speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: τήν is Helen: 'her'. This is the stock formula that introduces a reply by Telemachus, translated the same way each time: αὖ is 'in turn', ἀντίον 'face to face', and πεπνυμένος 'prudent' is his standing epithet. ηὔδα is the augmented imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak'.

sentences.t: οὕτω νῦν Ζεὺς θείη, ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης·
sentences.tr: houtō nyn Zeus theiē, erigdoupos posis Hērēs·
sentences.l: “So now may Zeus ordain, loud-crashing husband of Hera;
sentences.i: “So may Zeus now ordain it, loud-crashing husband of Hera;
sentences.n: οὕτω νῦν is 'so now', and θείη is the aorist optative of τίθημι, 'may he ordain', a wish: may it be as Helen has said. The object is left to be understood. ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης 'loud-crashing husband of Hera' is Zeus's descriptive phrase: ἐρίγδουπος is ἐρι- 'very' (here 'loud') + δοῦπος 'heavy crash', and a link with thunder is only the traditional reading. Ἥρης has Ionic η (Attic Ἥρας).

sentences.t: τῷ κέν τοι καὶ κεῖθι θεῷ ὣς εὐχετοῴμην.
sentences.tr: tōi ken toi kai keithi theōi hōs euchetoōimēn.
sentences.l: then to you, even there, as to a god, I would pray.”
sentences.i: then even there I would pray to you as to a god.”
sentences.n: τῷ is 'then, in that case'. κεν (= ἄν) with the optative gives 'would', and τοι is σοι, 'to you'. κεῖθι is the epic form of ἐκεῖ, 'there': away from Sparta; the place is not named, but the sense is presumably his own home. εὐχετοῴμην is the optative of εὐχετάομαι 'pray, make vows', with its vowels left uncontracted (diectasis; Attic εὐχετῴμην). Telemachus says that if Helen's reading comes true he will honour her as a god. The closing quotation mark ends his reply.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ ἐφ’ ἵπποιϊν μάστιν βάλεν·
sentences.tr: ē kai eph’ hippoiïn mastin balen·
sentences.l: He spoke, and upon the two horses a whip he laid;
sentences.i: So he said, and laid the whip on the horses;
sentences.n: ἦ καί is 'he spoke, and': ἦ is the old verb of saying, and it rounds off a speech before the action goes on. The subject of βάλεν is not named: ἦ has the speaker, Telemachus, as its subject, but the whip is the driver's, and the driver in this part is Peisistratus (199, 215), so the Greek leaves open who holds it. ἐφ’ is ἐπί before a rough-breathed word, and it takes the dative ἵπποιϊν, the dual 'the two horses' (Attic ἵπποιν). βάλεν is an aorist without augment, and μάστιν is the accusative of μάστιξ 'whip'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ μάλ’ ὦκα
ἤϊξαν πεδίονδε διὰ πτόλιος μεμαῶτες.
sentences.tr:
hoi de mal’ ōka
ēïxan pedionde dia ptolios memaōtes.
sentences.l:
and they very swiftly
darted to the plain through the city, eager.
sentences.i: and the horses darted very swiftly through the city to the plain, eager.
sentences.n: οἱ is 'they': the pair of horses, as the next line makes plain, though the pronoun is plural. ἤϊξαν is the aorist of ἀΐσσω 'dart, rush', and μάλ’ ὦκα 'very swiftly'. The -δε of πεδίονδε marks direction, 'to the plain'. πτόλιος is the genitive of πτόλις, the old by-form of πόλις. μεμαῶτες is the perfect participle of the Homeric μέμονα/μέμαα 'strive, be eager', masculine nominative plural.

sentences.t: οἱ δὲ πανημέριοι σεῖον ζυγὸν ἀμφὶς ἔχοντες.
sentences.tr: hoi de panēmerioi seion zygon amphis echontes.
sentences.l: And they all day long shook the yoke, holding it on either side.
sentences.i: All day long the horses shook the yoke that they bore between them.
sentences.n: This is a repeated line and keeps its English. πανημέριοι is 'all day long' (an adjective doing the work of an adverb); σεῖον is the imperfect of σείω 'shake', without augment. The yoke rests across the pair, and ἀμφὶς ἔχοντες 'holding it on either side' says that each horse carries one end of it.

sentences.t: δύσετό τ’ ἠέλιος σκιόωντό τε πᾶσαι ἀγυιαί·
sentences.tr: dyseto t’ ēelios skioōnto te pasai aguiai·
sentences.l: And the sun set, and all the streets grew shadowy.
sentences.i: The sun set, and all the streets grew dark.
sentences.n: This is the stock line that marks the fall of evening, and it keeps its English. δύσετο is an aorist middle of δύω 'set, sink' (here without augment); ἠέλιος is Ionic ἥλιος; σκιόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect of σκιάω 'darken' (Attic ἐσκιῶντο); ἀγυιαί are 'streets'.

sentences.t:
ἐς Φηρὰς δ’ ἵκοντο Διοκλῆος ποτὶ δῶμα,
υἱέος Ὀρτιλόχοιο, τὸν Ἀλφειὸς τέκε παῖδα.
sentences.tr:
es Phēras d’ hikonto Dioklēos poti dōma,
huieos Ortilochoio, ton Alpheios teke paida.
sentences.l:
and to Pherae they came, to the house of Diocles,
son of Ortilochus, whom Alpheus begot as his child.
sentences.i: and they came to Pherae, to the house of Diocles, son of Ortilochus, whom Alpheus begot.
sentences.n: Φηράς is Pherae, a town (accusative plural, after ἐς 'to'), and ἵκοντο is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι 'arrive at', without augment. Διοκλῆος and Ὀρτιλόχοιο are genitives; υἱέος is υἱοῦ, 'of the son'. Ἀλφειός is Alpheus, the river of the western Peloponnese, named here as father of Ortilochus. τέκε is the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω 'beget'. ποτί is πρός 'to'.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δὲ νύκτ’ ἄεσαν ὁ δὲ τοῖς πὰρ ξείνια θῆκεν.
sentences.tr: entha de nykt’ aesan ho de tois par xeinia thēken.
sentences.l: And there they slept the night, and he set beside them the things due to guests.
sentences.i: There they spent the night, and he set before them the hospitality due to guests.
sentences.n: ἄεσαν is the aorist of ἄω 'sleep, spend the night', third plural. No stop is printed in the middle of this line, but the clause breaks at ὁ δέ: ὁ is the pronoun 'he', Diocles, and τοῖς is 'to them'. πὰρ … θῆκεν is tmesis for παρέθηκεν 'set before'; ξείνια are 'the things due to guests', the hospitality owed to a guest-friend.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
ἵππους τε ζεύγνυντ’ ἀνά θ’ ἅρματα ποικίλ’ ἔβαινον,
ἐκ δ’ ἔλασαν προθύροιο καὶ αἰθούσης ἐριδούπου·
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
hippous te zeugnynt’ ana th’ harmata poikil’ ebainon,
ek d’ elasan prothyroio kai aithousēs eridoupou·
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, they yoked the horses and mounted the inlaid chariot, and drove out of the forecourt and the loud-echoing portico;
sentences.n: The first line is the stock line for daybreak, translated the same way each time: ἠριγένεια 'early-born' and ῥοδοδάκτυλος 'rose-fingered' are Dawn's standing epithets. ζεύγνυντ’ is the imperfect of ζεύγνυμι 'yoke', with an elided ending. ἀνά … ἔβαινον is tmesis for ἀνέβαινον 'mounted', and ἅρματα, though plural, is one chariot. ποικίλ’ is ποικίλα, 'inlaid' (the word means 'variegated', and for metal and wood work we say 'inlaid'). ἐκ … ἔλασαν is tmesis for 'drove out', from ἐλαύνω; προθύροιο is a genitive in -οιο, 'of the forecourt'; ἐριδούπου is 'loud-echoing', ἐρι- 'very, loud' + δοῦπος 'heavy sound'.

sentences.t: μάστιξεν δ’ ἐλάαν, τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἄκοντε πετέσθην.
sentences.tr: mastixen d’ elaan, tō d’ ouk akonte petesthēn.
sentences.l: and he whipped them to drive on, and the two, not unwilling, flew.
sentences.i: he whipped them to drive them on, and the pair flew not unwilling.
sentences.n: This line has been seen before and keeps its English. μάστιξεν is the aorist of μαστίζω 'whip' (without augment) and ἐλάαν the uncontracted infinitive of ἐλαύνω 'drive': 'whipped them to drive on'. τώ is the dual 'the two' (the horses). ἄκοντε is the dual of ἄκων, the contracted form of ἀέκων 'unwilling'; 'not unwilling' means eager. πετέσθην is a dual past tense of πέτομαι 'fly': the pair ran at full speed.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἔπειθ’ ἵκοντο Πύλου αἰπὺ πτολίεθρον·
sentences.tr: aipsa d’ epeith’ hikonto Pylou aipy ptoliethron·
sentences.l: and at once then they reached Pylos' steep citadel;
sentences.i: and at once they reached the steep citadel of Pylos;
sentences.n: αἶψα 'at once' and ἔπειθ’ 'then' together stress how quickly the drive went; ἔπειθ’ is ἔπειτα elided, with τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ἵκοντο. ἵκοντο is an aorist without augment. Πύλου is the genitive of Πύλος, Nestor's city. αἰπύ 'steep, sheer' agrees with πτολίεθρον 'citadel, town', an epic extension of πτόλις.

sentences.t: καὶ τότε Τηλέμαχος προσεφώνεε Νέστορος υἱόν·
sentences.tr: kai tote Tēlemachos prosephōnee Nestoros huion·
sentences.l: and then Telemachus spoke to Nestor's son:
sentences.i: and then Telemachus spoke to the son of Nestor:
sentences.n: προσεφώνεε is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω 'speak to'. Νέστορος υἱόν is Peisistratus, named by his father here and addressed by the patronymic in the next line. Telemachus's speech follows.

sentences.t:
Νεστορίδη, πῶς κέν μοι ὑποσχόμενος τελέσειας
μῦθον ἐμόν;
sentences.tr:
Nestoridē, pōs ken moi hyposchomenos teleseias
mython emon;
sentences.l:
“Son of Nestor, how might you, for me, having promised,
fulfil my word?
sentences.i: “Son of Nestor, how might you promise me and then fulfil my request?
sentences.n: Νεστορίδη is the vocative of the patronymic 'son of Nestor', a polite address to Peisistratus. πῶς κεν with the optative asks 'how might …?'. ὑποσχόμενος is the aorist middle participle of ὑπισχνέομαι 'promise, undertake', and τελέσειας the aorist optative of τελέω 'fulfil, carry out'. μῦθον ἐμόν is 'my word', here what Telemachus is about to ask: the request comes in the lines that follow. The Greek question mark is the semicolon.

sentences.t:
ξεῖνοι δὲ διαμπερὲς εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι
ἐκ πατέρων φιλότητος, ἀτὰρ καὶ ὁμήλικές εἰμεν·
sentences.tr:
xeinoi de diamperes euchometh’ einai
ek paterōn philotētos, atar kai homēlikes eimen·
sentences.l:
and guest-friends continually we declare ourselves to be
from our fathers' friendship, and moreover of like age we are;
sentences.i: We declare ourselves guest-friends without a break, through our fathers' friendship, and we are also of an age;
sentences.n: ξεῖνοι are 'guest-friends', bound by the hereditary tie of hospitality, and εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι is 'we declare ourselves to be', from εὔχομαι, which means 'claim, declare' as well as 'pray'. διαμπερές is 'continually, right through', and ἐκ πατέρων φιλότητος 'from our fathers' friendship' says where the bond comes from. ἀτὰρ καί is 'and moreover'. ὁμήλικες are 'of the same age', and εἰμεν is the epic first plural of εἰμί (Attic ἐσμέν).

sentences.t: ἥδε δ’ ὁδὸς καὶ μᾶλλον ὁμοφροσύνῃσιν ἐνήσει.
sentences.tr: hēde d’ hodos kai mallon homophrosynēisin enēsei.
sentences.l: and this road even more into like-mindedness will put (us).
sentences.i: and this journey will bring us still closer in accord.
sentences.n: ὁμοφροσύνῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν of ὁμοφροσύνη 'like-mindedness, concord', plural for an abstract. ἐνήσει is the future of ἐνίημι 'send into, put into'. The Greek leaves out the object: 'us' is understood, and the literal sense is 'will put us still further into concord'. The construction is elliptical, but the meaning is plain: the road they share will strengthen their friendship. ἥδε is 'this', the road they have been travelling together.

sentences.t:
μή με παρὲξ ἄγε νῆα, διοτρεφές, ἀλλὰ λίπ’ αὐτοῦ,
μή μ’ ὁ γέρων ἀέκοντα κατάσχῃ ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
ἱέμενος φιλέειν·
sentences.tr:
mē me parex age nēa, diotrephes, alla lip’ autou,
mē m’ ho gerōn aekonta kataschēi hōi eni oikōi
hiemenos phileein·
sentences.i: Do not take me past the ship, Zeus-nurtured one, but leave me right here, lest the old man detain me against my will in his own house, in his eagerness to welcome me;
sentences.n: Telemachus asks to be left at the ship rather than carried on to Nestor's house. παρέξ is 'past, beyond', here with the accusative νῆα, and ἄγε is the imperative of ἄγω. λίπ’ is λίπε, the aorist imperative of λείπω 'leave', with 'me' understood, and αὐτοῦ is the adverb 'right here, on the spot'. διοτρεφές 'Zeus-nurtured' is an honorific for a man of a royal house, here Peisistratus. μή with the aorist subjunctive κατάσχῃ means 'lest he hold me back' (κατέχω 'detain'). ὁ γέρων is Nestor, 'the old man'; ἀέκοντα 'unwilling' agrees with μ’ (με); ᾧ is the possessive 'his own', not the relative; ἱέμενος is 'eager', and φιλέειν the uncontracted infinitive of φιλέω, here 'to welcome as a guest'.

sentences.t: ἐμὲ δὲ χρεὼ θᾶσσον ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.tr: eme de chreō thasson hikesthai.
sentences.l: and for me there is need to arrive more quickly.”
sentences.i: and I have need to arrive more quickly.”
sentences.n: χρεώ is 'need', with ἐστί understood, and the accusative ἐμέ and the infinitive ἱκέσθαι: 'there is need for me to arrive'. θᾶσσον is the comparative adverb of ταχύς, 'more quickly, sooner', and ἱκέσθαι the aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι 'arrive'. The place he must reach is not named; the context makes it Ithaca. The closing quotation mark ends Telemachus's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Νεστορίδης δ’ ἄρ’ ἑῷ συμφράσσατο θυμῷ,
ὅππως οἱ κατὰ μοῖραν ὑποσχόμενος τελέσειεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Nestoridēs d’ ar’ heōi symphrassato thymōi,
hoppōs hoi kata moiran hyposchomenos teleseien.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Nestor's son then in his own heart considered,
how to him as is fitting, having promised, he might fulfil it.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the son of Nestor considered in his own heart how he might promise him and fulfil it as is fitting.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο 'So he spoke' closes Telemachus's speech. Νεστορίδης is the patronymic standing for Peisistratus, and ἑῷ is the possessive 'his own'. συμφράσσατο is the aorist middle of συμφράζομαι 'consider, deliberate', here with himself. ὅππως is ὅπως 'how', with the optative τελέσειεν in an indirect question; οἱ is 'to him', Telemachus, and κατὰ μοῖραν is 'as is fitting'. ὑποσχόμενος … τελέσειεν takes up Telemachus's own words in line 195.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ οἱ φρονέοντι δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι·
sentences.tr: hōde de hoi phroneonti doassato kerdion einai·
sentences.l: And thus to him considering it seemed better to be:
sentences.i: And this, as he thought it over, seemed to him the better course:
sentences.n: ὧδε 'thus' points forward to the plan in the next lines. φρονέοντι is the uncontracted dative participle of φρονέω 'think, consider': 'to him thinking'. δοάσσατο is an epic aorist 'it seemed', and κέρδιον is a comparative built on the stem of κέρδος 'gain': 'better, more advantageous'.

sentences.t:
στρέψ’ ἵππους ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν καὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης,
νηῒ δ’ ἐνὶ πρύμνῃ ἐξαίνυτο κάλλιμα δῶρα,
ἐσθῆτα χρυσόν τε, τά οἱ Μενέλαος ἔδωκε·
sentences.tr:
streps’ hippous epi nēa thoēn kai thina thalassēs,
nēï d’ eni prymnēi exainyto kallima dōra,
esthēta chryson te, ta hoi Menelaos edōke·
sentences.i: he turned the horses toward the swift ship and the shore of the sea, and in the stern of the ship unloaded the fair gifts, the clothing and the gold that Menelaus had given him;
sentences.n: The subject is the son of Nestor, as in line 202. στρέψ’ is στρέψε, the aorist of στρέφω 'turn', without augment and with its vowel elided. ἐξαίνυτο is the imperfect middle of ἐξαίνυμαι 'take out': the gifts come out of the chariot, and νηῒ … πρύμνῃ 'in the ship, at the stern' is a locative (ἐνί with the dative) that says where he does it; the Greek does not name the chariot or say 'put', but the sense is that he takes the gifts out of the chariot and sets them at the stern. κάλλιμα δῶρα are 'fair gifts' (κάλλιμα is from κάλλος 'beauty'). ἐσθῆτα χρυσόν τε 'clothing and gold' say what the gifts were; τά is the relative 'which', and οἱ 'to him', Telemachus. θῖνα θαλάσσης is 'the shore of the sea'.

sentences.t: καί μιν ἐποτρύνων ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: kai min epotrynōn epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and, urging him on, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and, urging him on, spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: ἐποτρύνων is the present participle of ἐποτρύνω 'urge on, press', and μιν is 'him', Telemachus. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the stock introduction to a speech, translated the same way each time; προσηύδα is the augmented imperfect of προσαυδάω 'speak to'. Peisistratus's speech follows.

sentences.t:
σπουδῇ νῦν ἀνάβαινε κέλευέ τε πάντας ἑταίρους,
πρὶν ἐμὲ οἴκαδ’ ἱκέσθαι ἀπαγγεῖλαί τε γέροντι.
sentences.tr:
spoudēi nyn anabaine keleue te pantas hetairous,
prin eme oikad’ hikesthai apangeilai te geronti.
sentences.l:
“In haste now go aboard and bid all your companions,
before I reach home and report to the old man.
sentences.i: “Now go aboard in haste, and give orders to all your companions, before I reach home and report to the old man.
sentences.n: σπουδῇ is 'in haste' (dative of manner). ἀνάβαινε is the imperative of ἀναβαίνω 'go up, go aboard', and κέλευε the imperative of κελεύω 'order, bid'; ἑταίρους are Telemachus's crew. πρίν takes the accusative and infinitive: ἐμὲ … ἱκέσθαι 'before I arrive' (Peisistratus's own home, Nestor's house) and ἀπαγγεῖλαι 'report', with γέροντι 'to the old man', Nestor, in the dative.

sentences.t: εὖ γὰρ ἐγὼ τόδε οἶδα κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν·
sentences.tr: eu gar egō tode oida kata phrena kai kata thymon·
sentences.l: for well I know this in mind and in heart:
sentences.i: For I know this well, in my mind and heart:
sentences.n: γάρ gives his reason for urging haste, and ἐγώ is stressed: 'I, who know the man'. οἶδα is a perfect with present sense, 'I know'; τόδε 'this' points forward to the next lines. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν is 'in mind and in heart', a paired phrase.

sentences.t:
οἷος κείνου θυμὸς ὑπέρβιος, οὔ σε μεθήσει,
ἀλλ’ αὐτὸς καλέων δεῦρ’ εἴσεται, οὐδέ ἕ φημι
ἂψ ἰέναι κενεόν·
sentences.tr:
hoios keinou thymos hyperbios, ou se methēsei,
all’ autos kaleōn deur’ eisetai, oude he phēmi
aps ienai keneon·
sentences.i: how overbearing that man's spirit is: he will not let you go, but will come here himself to summon you, and I say that he will not go back empty-handed;
sentences.n: οἷος is 'of what sort', and the clause says what the speaker knows about Nestor: ὑπέρβιος 'overweening, overbearing' (ὑπέρ 'over' + βία 'force'). κείνου is the epic form of ἐκείνου, 'that man's'. μεθήσει is the future of μεθίημι 'let go', and σε 'you'. καλέων is the uncontracted participle of καλέω 'call, summon', and εἴσεται is spelled like the future of οἶδα 'know', but with δεῦρ’ it can only be the Homeric future of εἶμι 'go', so δεῦρ’ εἴσεται is 'he will come here'. οὐδέ … φημι is 'and I say that … not', with the infinitive ἰέναι 'go'; ἕ is the accusative 'him', subject of the infinitive, and κενεόν 'empty' agrees with it: he will not go back without Telemachus.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ κεχολώσεται ἔμπης.
sentences.tr: mala gar kecholōsetai empēs.
sentences.l: for he will be very angry, all the same.”
sentences.i: for he will be very angry all the same.”
sentences.n: κεχολώσεται is a future perfect of χολόομαι 'be angry', 'he will be angry' (the perfect stem gives a settled state). ἔμπης is 'all the same, in any case'. The closing quotation mark ends Peisistratus's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἔλασεν καλλίτριχας ἵππους
ἂψ Πυλίων εἰς ἄστυ, θοῶς δ’ ἄρα δώμαθ’ ἵκανε.
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas elasen kallitrichas hippous
aps Pyliōn eis asty, thoōs d’ ara dōmath’ hikane.
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, he drove the fair-maned horses
back to the town of the Pylians, and swiftly then to the halls he came.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and drove the fair-maned horses back to the town of the Pylians, and quickly reached the halls.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας 'So then having spoken' closes a speech with the speaker's action following; the subject is Peisistratus. ἔλασεν is the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'drive', and καλλίτριχας 'fair-maned' is from καλλι- 'fair' + τρίχ- 'hair'. ἄψ is 'back', Πυλίων the genitive plural 'of the Pylians', and ἄστυ 'town'. δώμαθ’ is δώματα, 'house, halls' (a plural for one building), and ἵκανε is the epic imperfect of ἱκάνω 'reach'.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἐποτρύνων ἐκέλευσεν·
sentences.tr: Tēlemachos d’ hetaroisin epotrynōn ekeleusen·
sentences.l: And Telemachus, urging them on, gave orders to his companions:
sentences.i: And Telemachus gave orders to his companions, urging them on:
sentences.n: ἑτάροισιν is the dative plural of ἕταρος, the by-form of ἑταῖρος 'companion'. ἐποτρύνων 'urging on' and ἐκέλευσεν 'gave orders' (aorist of κελεύω) belong together; the colon announces the speech.

sentences.t:
ἐγκοσμεῖτε τὰ τεύχε’, ἑταῖροι, νηῒ μελαίνῃ,
αὐτοί τ’ ἀμβαίνωμεν, ἵνα πρήσσωμεν ὁδοῖο.
sentences.tr:
enkosmeite ta teuche’, hetairoi, nēï melainēi,
autoi t’ ambainōmen, hina prēssōmen hodoio.
sentences.l:
“Set in order the gear, companions, in the black ship,
and let us ourselves embark, so that we may make headway on our road.”
sentences.i: “Stow the gear in the black ship, companions, and let us go aboard ourselves, so that we may make headway on our road.”
sentences.n: ἐγκοσμεῖτε is the imperative of ἐγκοσμέω 'set in order in', here 'stow'. τεύχε’ is τεύχεα, 'gear, equipment' (the word also means 'arms'). νηῒ μελαίνῃ is the dative 'in the black ship'. αὐτοί is 'ourselves', and ἀμβαίνωμεν is the hortatory subjunctive of ἀναβαίνω with its preverb reduced to ἀμ- before β (ἀνα- becomes ἀμ-). ἵνα with the subjunctive gives purpose; πρήσσωμεν (= πράσσωμεν) with the genitive ὁδοῖο is 'make headway on the road'. The closing quotation mark ends Telemachus's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδ’ ἐπίθοντο,
αἶψα δ’ ἄρ’ εἴσβαινον καὶ ἐπὶ κληῗσι καθῖζον.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara tou mala men klyon ēd’ epithonto,
aipsa d’ ar’ eisbainon kai epi klēïsi kathizon.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then readily heard him and obeyed,
and at once then they went aboard and upon the rowing-benches sat down.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed, and at once went aboard and sat down at the oarlocks.
sentences.n: The first line is a stock line for obedience and keeps its English. ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο 'he spoke', elided (τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of οἱ). κλύον is 'heard' (κλύω, without augment), with the genitive τοῦ, 'him', because verbs of hearing take the genitive of the person; ἐπίθοντο is the aorist middle of πείθομαι 'obey'. εἴσβαινον is the imperfect of εἰσβαίνω 'go aboard', and καθῖζον the imperfect of καθίζω 'sit down'. κληῗσι is the dative plural of κληΐς, the word for the rowing-benches (or the thole-pins at them).

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὁ μὲν τὰ πονεῖτο καὶ εὔχετο, θῦε δ’ Ἀθήνῃ
νηῒ πάρα πρυμνῇ·
sentences.tr:
ē toi ho men ta poneito kai eucheto, thye d’ Athēnēi
nēï para prymnēi·
sentences.l:
Now he, for his part, was busy with these things and was praying, and sacrificed to Athena
beside the ship's stern;
sentences.i: Meanwhile he was busy with these things, praying and sacrificing to Athena beside the stern of the ship;
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is 'truly, now', and ὁ μέν 'he for his part' sets Telemachus against the crew of the last unit; the δέ of the next unit brings in the new arrival. πονεῖτο is the imperfect middle of πονέομαι 'toil, busy oneself', with τά 'these things' (the preparations). εὔχετο is the imperfect of εὔχομαι 'pray', and θῦε the imperfect of θύω 'sacrifice', with the dative Ἀθήνῃ (Ionic η). νηῒ πάρα πρυμνῇ is 'beside the ship's stern': πάρα is παρά placed after its noun, with the accent drawn back.

sentences.t:
σχεδόθεν δέ οἱ ἤλυθεν ἀνὴρ
τηλεδαπός, φεύγων ἐξ Ἄργεος ἄνδρα κατακτάς,
μάντις·
sentences.tr:
schedothen de hoi ēlythen anēr
tēledapos, pheugōn ex Argeos andra kataktas,
mantis·
sentences.i: and a man came up to him from close by, from a far-off land, in flight from Argos after killing a man: a seer;
sentences.n: σχεδόθεν 'from close by' has the -θεν of 'from'; οἱ is 'to him', Telemachus; ἤλυθεν is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι 'came' (Attic ἦλθεν). The man is not named until line 256. τηλεδαπός is 'from a far-off land'. φεύγων ἐξ Ἄργεος is 'fleeing out of Argos' (Ἄργεος is the genitive of Ἄργος), and κατακτάς is the aorist participle of κατακτείνω 'kill', a Homeric short form: 'having killed'. He is a manslayer in exile. μάντις 'seer' ends the unit at the stop printed after it.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ γενεήν γε Μελάμποδος ἔκγονος ἦεν,
ὃς πρὶν μέν ποτ’ ἔναιε Πύλῳ ἔνι, μητέρι μήλων,
ἀφνειὸς Πυλίοισι μέγ’ ἔξοχα δώματα ναίων·
sentences.tr:
atar geneēn ge Melampodos ekgonos ēen,
hos prin men pot’ enaie Pylōi eni, mēteri mēlōn,
aphneios Pylioisi meg’ exocha dōmata naiōn·
sentences.i: but he was by birth a descendant of Melampus, who formerly lived in Pylos, mother of flocks, a man pre-eminently rich among the Pylians, dwelling in his halls;
sentences.n: γενεήν γε is an accusative of respect, 'as to birth', and Μελάμποδος is the genitive 'of Melampus'; ἔκγονος is 'descendant', and ἦεν is ἦν. ὅς 'who' is Melampus. πρίν is the adverb 'formerly', with μέν ποτ’ 'once', and sets up δὴ τότε 'then indeed' in the next unit. ἔναιε is the imperfect of ναίω 'dwell'; ἔνι is ἐν placed after its noun, with the accent drawn back; Πύλῳ is the dative of place. μητέρι μήλων 'mother of flocks' calls Pylos a land that breeds flocks. ἀφνειός is 'rich'. μέγ’ ἔξοχα are adverbs, 'greatly' and 'pre-eminently' (ἔξοχος 'standing out', here above the other Pylians); they could instead go with the halls, but here they are taken with ἀφνειός. δώματα is a plural for one house.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότε γ’ ἄλλων δῆμον ἀφίκετο, πατρίδα φεύγων
Νηλέα τε μεγάθυμον, ἀγαυότατον ζωόντων,
ὅς οἱ χρήματα πολλὰ τελεσφόρον εἰς ἐνιαυτὸν
εἶχε βίῃ.
sentences.tr:
dē tote g’ allōn dēmon aphiketo, patrida pheugōn
Nēlea te megathymon, agauotaton zōontōn,
hos hoi chrēmata polla telesphoron eis eniauton
eiche biēi.
sentences.l:
then indeed to the land of others he came, fleeing his fatherland,
and to great-hearted Neleus, most noble of the living,
who his many goods for a completion-bearing year
held by force.
sentences.i: Then indeed he came to the land of others, fleeing his fatherland, and to great-hearted Neleus, the most noble of the living, who held his many possessions by force for a full year.
sentences.n: δὴ τότε γ’ is 'then indeed', answering πρὶν μέν ποτ’ of the last unit. ἄλλων δῆμον is 'the land of others', δῆμος being 'land'. ἀφίκετο is the aorist of ἀφικνέομαι 'come to', and it takes both δῆμον and Νηλέα 'to Neleus'. πατρίδα 'fatherland' is the object of φεύγων. μεγάθυμος is 'great-hearted'; ἀγαυότατον is the superlative of ἀγαυός 'noble', and ζωόντων the uncontracted genitive plural participle of ζώω 'live'. In ὅς οἱ …, ὅς is Neleus and οἱ is 'his', the dative of possession for Melampus; τελεσφόρον εἰς ἐνιαυτόν is 'for a full year' (τελεσφόρος 'bringing to completion'), and εἶχε βίῃ 'held by force'.

sentences.t:
ὁ δὲ τῆος ἐνὶ μεγάροις Φυλάκοιο
δεσμῷ ἐν ἀργαλέῳ δέδετο, κρατέρ’ ἄλγεα πάσχων
εἵνεκα Νηλῆος κούρης ἄτης τε βαρείης,
τήν οἱ ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε θεὰ δασπλῆτις Ἐρινύς.
sentences.tr:
ho de tēos eni megarois Phylakoio
desmōi en argaleōi dedeto, krater’ algea paschōn
heineka Nēlēos kourēs atēs te bareiēs,
tēn hoi epi phresi thēke thea dasplētis Erinys.
sentences.l:
and he meanwhile in the halls of Phylacus
in a bond, a grievous one, was bound, suffering strong pains
on account of the daughter of Neleus and of heavy ruin,
which upon his mind put the goddess, the terrible Erinys.
sentences.i: Meanwhile he lay bound in a grievous bond in the halls of Phylacus, suffering severe pains on account of the daughter of Neleus and a heavy ruin, which the terrible goddess Erinys had put upon his mind.
sentences.n: ὁ δέ 'but he' is Melampus, set against Neleus. τῆος is τέως 'meanwhile', μεγάροις 'halls', and Φυλάκοιο the genitive 'of Phylacus'. δέδετο is the pluperfect passive of δέω 'bind': 'he was bound'. δεσμῷ ἐν ἀργαλέῳ is 'in a grievous bond', and κρατέρ’ is κρατερά 'strong', agreeing with ἄλγεα 'pains'. εἵνεκα (= ἕνεκα) 'on account of' governs both Νηλῆος κούρης 'the daughter of Neleus' and ἄτης … βαρείης 'heavy ruin'. ἄτη is the blindness of mind that leads to ruin; here the goddess puts it on his mind, so the word covers both his delusion and the disaster. τήν is the relative 'which' (ἄτην), and οἱ 'to him'; ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε is 'put upon his mind'. δασπλῆτις is an epithet of Erinys of uncertain meaning; 'terrible' is the traditional guess. The Erinys is a goddess of vengeance.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἔκφυγε κῆρα καὶ ἤλασε βοῦς ἐριμύκους
ἐς Πύλον ἐκ Φυλάκης καὶ ἐτίσατο ἔργον ἀεικὲς
ἀντίθεον Νηλῆα, κασιγνήτῳ δὲ γυναῖκα
ἠγάγετο πρὸς δώμαθ’.
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men ekphyge kēra kai ēlase bous erimykous
es Pylon ek Phylakēs kai etisato ergon aeikes
antitheon Nēlēa, kasignētōi de gynaika
ēgageto pros dōmath’.
sentences.l:
But he escaped death-fate, and drove the loud-lowing cattle
to Pylos from Phylace, and took vengeance for the unseemly deed
on godlike Neleus, and for his brother a wife
he led to the halls.
sentences.i: But he escaped death, and drove the loud-lowing cattle from Phylace to Pylos, and took vengeance for the unseemly deed on godlike Neleus, and brought a wife home for his brother.
sentences.n: ὁ μέν is Melampus again. ἔκφυγε is the aorist of ἐκφεύγω 'escape', without augment, and κῆρα is the accusative of κήρ 'death, the doom of death', a different word from κῆρ 'heart'. ἤλασε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'drive'; ἐριμύκους 'loud-lowing' is ἐρι- 'very, loud' + μυκάομαι 'low'. ἐτίσατο is the aorist middle of τίνω 'exact a penalty', with ἔργον ἀεικές 'the unseemly deed' and Νηλῆα 'Neleus' as its objects: 'took vengeance on Neleus for the deed'. ἀντίθεος is 'godlike'. κασιγνήτῳ is 'for his brother', and ἠγάγετο the middle aorist of ἄγω, the verb for leading a bride home, here for his brother (κασιγνήτῳ), not for himself. The text says only γυναῖκα 'a wife'; she is understood to be the daughter of Neleus named above. δώμαθ’ is δώματα, a plural for one house.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄλλων ἵκετο δῆμον,
Ἄργος ἐς ἱππόβοτον·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ allōn hiketo dēmon,
Argos es hippoboton·
sentences.l:
and he came to the land of others,
to Argos, horse-pasturing;
sentences.i: and he came to the land of others, to horse-pasturing Argos;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ is Melampus. ἄλλων δῆμον 'the land of others' repeats the phrase of line 228, now with a new destination. ἵκετο is an aorist without augment. ἱππόβοτος 'horse-pasturing' is an epithet of Argos: ἵππος 'horse' + βόσκω 'feed, pasture'.

sentences.t:
τόθι γάρ νύ οἱ αἴσιμον ἦεν
ναιέμεναι πολλοῖσιν ἀνάσσοντ’ Ἀργείοισιν
ἔνθα δ’ ἔγημε γυναῖκα καὶ ὑψερεφὲς θέτο δῶμα,
γείνατο δ’ Ἀντιφάτην καὶ Μάντιον, υἷε κραταιώ.
sentences.tr:
tothi gar ny hoi aisimon ēen
naiemenai polloisin anassont’ Argeioisin
entha d’ egēme gynaika kai hypserephes theto dōma,
geinato d’ Antiphatēn kai Mantion, huie krataiō.
sentences.l:
for there it was fated for him
to dwell, ruling over many Argives;
there he married a wife and set up a high-roofed house,
and begot Antiphates and Mantius, two strong sons.
sentences.i: for it was fated that he should live there, ruling over many Argives; and there he married a wife and built a high-roofed house, and begot Antiphates and Mantius, two strong sons.
sentences.n: τόθι is the epic adverb 'there'; γάρ gives the reason for his going to Argos; οἱ is 'to him'. αἴσιμον ἦεν is 'it was fated, it was his due', with the infinitive ναιέμεναι (the Homeric ending -έμεναι, from ναίω 'dwell'); ἀνάσσοντ’ is a participle 'ruling', with the dative Ἀργείοισιν 'over the Argives'. No stop is printed at the end of line 240, but a new statement begins with ἔνθα δ’. ἔγημε is the aorist of γαμέω, said of a man: 'took a wife'. ὑψερεφές is 'high-roofed', and θέτο the aorist middle of τίθημι, 'set up, built'. γείνατο is the aorist middle of γείνομαι, said of a father: 'begot'. υἷε is the dual of υἱός 'son', and κραταιώ the dual of κραταιός, a by-form of κρατερός 'strong'.

sentences.t:
Ἀντιφάτης μὲν ἔτικτεν Ὀϊκλῆα μεγάθυμον,
αὐτὰρ Ὀϊκλείης λαοσσόον Ἀμφιάραον,
ὃν περὶ κῆρι φίλει Ζεύς τ’ αἰγίοχος καὶ Ἀπόλλων
παντοίην φιλότητ’·
sentences.tr:
Antiphatēs men etikten Oïklēa megathymon,
autar Oïkleiēs laossoon Amphiaraon,
hon peri kēri philei Zeus t’ aigiochos kai Apollōn
pantoiēn philotēt’·
sentences.l:
Antiphates fathered great-hearted Oicles,
and Oicles, people-rousing Amphiaraus,
whom aegis-bearing Zeus and Apollo loved exceedingly in heart
with every kind of love;
sentences.i: Antiphates fathered great-hearted Oicles, and Oicles fathered Amphiaraus, rouser of the people, whom aegis-bearing Zeus and Apollo loved exceedingly in their hearts, with every kind of love;
sentences.n: μέν … αὐτάρ marks the two generations; ἔτικτεν is the imperfect of τίκτω 'beget, father', and it is understood again with Ὀϊκλείης, which is a nominative (the accusative is Ὀϊκλῆα). μεγάθυμος is 'great-hearted'. λαοσσόος is 'rousing the people' (λαός 'people' + σεύω 'rouse, drive on'); the ancients also took it as 'saving the people', so the derivation is disputed. ὃν περὶ κῆρι φίλει: ὅν is the relative 'whom', περί the adverb 'exceedingly', κῆρι the dative of κῆρ 'heart', and φίλει the imperfect of φιλέω 'love', in the singular with the nearer subject Ζεύς. αἰγίοχος is 'aegis-bearing', meaning disputed. παντοίην φιλότητ’ is 'every kind of love', an accusative of the thing felt.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἵκετο γήραος οὐδόν,
ἀλλ’ ὄλετ’ ἐν Θήβῃσι γυναίων εἵνεκα δώρων.
sentences.tr:
oud’ hiketo gēraos oudon,
all’ olet’ en Thēbēisi gynaiōn heineka dōrōn.
sentences.l:
and he did not reach the threshold of old age,
but perished in Thebes on account of women's gifts.
sentences.i: and he never reached the threshold of old age, but perished at Thebes because of women's gifts.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἵκετο γήραος οὐδόν is 'and he did not reach the threshold of old age': old age is a doorway he never crossed. γήραος is the genitive of γῆρας. ὄλετ’ is the aorist middle of ὄλλυμι, 'perished'. Θήβῃσι is a dative plural of Θῆβαι, 'at Thebes'. εἵνεκα 'because of' governs γυναίων δώρων, 'women's gifts', an adjective formed from γυνή. The line hints at the gift that won over Amphiaraus's wife; the story is not told here.

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ υἱεῖς ἐγένοντ’ Ἀλκμαίων Ἀμφίλοχός τε.
sentences.tr: tou d’ huieis egenont’ Alkmaiōn Amphilochos te.
sentences.l: And of him sons were born, Alcmaeon and Amphilochus.
sentences.i: And his sons were Alcmaeon and Amphilochus.
sentences.n: τοῦ is 'of him', Amphiaraus. υἱεῖς is the nominative plural of υἱός, and ἐγένοντ’ is the elided aorist of γίγνομαι, third plural, 'were born'. Ἀλκμαίων and Ἀμφίλοχος stand in apposition to 'sons'. This line closes Amphiaraus's branch of the family.

sentences.t: Μάντιος αὖ τέκετο Πολυφείδεά τε Κλεῖτόν τε·
sentences.tr: Mantios au teketo Polypheidea te Kleiton te·
sentences.l: Mantius, in his turn, begot Polypheides and Cleitus;
sentences.i: Mantius, in his turn, begot Polypheides and Cleitus;
sentences.n: Μάντιος is a nominative, 'Mantius', one of the two sons of line 242 (the accusative was Μάντιον). αὖ 'in turn' passes to the other branch. τέκετο is the unaugmented aorist middle of τίκτω, said of a father: 'begot'. Πολυφείδεά and Κλεῖτον are accusatives; the line has two names joined by τε … τε. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the last syllable of τέκετο has to count long before Πολυφείδεά (the longum of the third foot), and the fifth foot is a spondee (τε Κλεῖ).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι Κλεῖτον χρυσόθρονος ἥρπασεν Ἠὼς
κάλλεος εἵνεκα οἷο, ἵν’ ἀθανάτοισι μετείη·
sentences.tr:
all’ ē toi Kleiton chrysothronos hērpasen Ēōs
kalleos heineka hoio, hin’ athanatoisi meteiē·
sentences.l:
but truly Cleitus golden-throned Dawn snatched away
on account of his own beauty, that he might be among the immortals;
sentences.i: but golden-throned Dawn snatched Cleitus away for the sake of his beauty, so that he might be among the immortals;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι is 'but indeed', setting Cleitus's fate against Amphiaraus's. ἥρπασεν is the same verb, ἁρπάζω, as the eagle's snatching of the goose in line 174; here it is a goddess carrying off a mortal. χρυσόθρονος Ἠώς is 'golden-throned Dawn' (θρόνος 'seat'; an old alternative takes the second part as θρόνα 'embroidered flowers'). κάλλεος is the uncontracted genitive of κάλλος 'beauty', with εἵνεκα 'because of'; οἷο is the possessive genitive 'his own'. ἵν’ is ἵνα 'so that', with the optative μετείη, from μέτειμι 'be among'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὑπέρθυμον Πολυφείδεα μάντιν Ἀπόλλων
θῆκε βροτῶν ὄχ’ ἄριστον, ἐπεὶ θάνεν Ἀμφιάραος·
sentences.tr:
autar hyperthymon Polypheidea mantin Apollōn
thēke brotōn och’ ariston, epei thanen Amphiaraos·
sentences.l:
but high-spirited Polypheides, a seer, Apollo
made by far the best of mortals, after Amphiaraus died;
sentences.i: but Apollo made high-spirited Polypheides, the seer, by far the best of mortals after Amphiaraus died;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ 'but' turns to the second brother. ὑπέρθυμος is 'high-spirited', and μάντιν 'seer' is in apposition to Πολυφείδεα. θῆκε 'made' takes two accusatives, the man and βροτῶν ὄχ’ ἄριστον 'best of mortals by far' (ὄχ’ is ὄχα 'by far', elided, with the superlative; βροτῶν is a partitive genitive). θάνεν is the aorist of θνῄσκω 'die', without augment.

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥ’ Ὑπερησίηνδ’ ἀπενάσσατο πατρὶ χολωθείς,
ἔνθ’ ὅ γε ναιετάων μαντεύετο πᾶσι βροτοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
hos rh’ Hyperēsiēnd’ apenassato patri cholōtheis,
enth’ ho ge naietaōn manteueto pasi brotoisin.
sentences.l:
who to Hypereisia removed himself, angered at his father,
and there, dwelling, prophesied to all mortals.
sentences.i: He moved away to Hypereisia, angry with his father, and there he lived and prophesied to all mortals.
sentences.n: ὅς is Polypheides, and πατρί is his father Mantius (249). ὅς ῥ’ is ὅς ῥα, the particle ῥα adding 'as one would expect'. Ὑπερησίηνδ’ is Ὑπερησίην with the -δε of direction, 'to Hypereisia', a place name. ἀπενάσσατο is the aorist middle of ἀπονάσσω, 'settle away, remove one's dwelling'. πατρὶ χολωθείς is 'angered at his father', the aorist passive participle of χολόω with a dative of cause. ἔνθ’ ὅ γε is 'there he'; ναιετάων is the uncontracted participle of ναιετάω 'dwell', and μαντεύετο the imperfect middle of μαντεύομαι 'prophesy', with the dative πᾶσι βροτοῖσιν 'to all mortals'.

sentences.t:
τοῦ μὲν ἄρ’ υἱὸς ἐπῆλθε, Θεοκλύμενος δ’ ὄνομ’ ἦεν,
ὃς τότε Τηλεμάχου πέλας ἵστατο·
sentences.tr:
tou men ar’ huios epēlthe, Theoklymenos d’ onom’ ēen,
hos tote Tēlemachou pelas histato·
sentences.l:
Of him then a son came up, and Theoclymenus was his name,
who then stood near Telemachus;
sentences.i: His son then came up, Theoclymenus by name, and stood near Telemachus;
sentences.n: τοῦ is 'of him', Polypheides, the seer just described, and μὲν ἄρ’ 'so then' ties the family history back to the scene. ἐπῆλθε is the aorist of ἐπέρχομαι 'come up'. Θεοκλύμενος is the stranger of line 223: the seer from Argos is now named, and the genealogy has shown him a descendant of Melampus. ὄνομ’ is ὄνομα, and ἦεν is ἦν. πέλας is 'near', with the genitive Τηλεμάχου, and ἵστατο the imperfect middle of ἵστημι 'stand'.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐκίχανεν
σπένδοντ’ εὐχόμενόν τε θοῇ παρὰ νηῒ μελαίνῃ,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ekichanen
spendont’ euchomenon te thoēi para nēï melainēi,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
and him he came upon
pouring a libation and praying beside the swift black ship,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and found him pouring a libation and praying beside the swift black ship, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: ἐκίχανεν is a past tense of κιχάνω 'come upon, find'. σπένδοντ’ and εὐχόμενον are present participles agreeing with τόν, Telemachus: 'pouring a libation and praying', as at the stern in 222–223. θοῇ παρὰ νηῒ μελαίνῃ is 'beside the swift black ship', the full formula for the ship. καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the stock introduction to a speech, with φωνήσας 'lifting his voice'. Theoclymenus's speech follows in the next part, and its opening quotation mark is printed there.
